title: NEC Past Paper - Set 18 (2083 Asoj 18, 1st shift)

questions.q: A Bheri-type settling basin in a run-of-river scheme is used to:
o: Settle out suspended sediment before the water enters the penstock
Store water to meet the evening peak
Dissipate the energy of the diverted flow
Measure the discharge entering the headrace
questions.s: The flow is slowed in a widened basin so that sand above the design particle size falls out before it can abrade the turbine runner.
questions.trap: A forebay is also a widened pond on the waterway, but it balances supply and demand rather than removing sediment.
questions.trick: Slow the water down and the sand drops out.

questions.q: The minimum velocity kept in a high-head penstock is governed by the need to:
o: Keep sediment in suspension and avoid deposition
Limit the thickness of the steel shell
questions.s: Too low a velocity lets silt settle inside the pipe. The upper limit is set by friction loss and surge, which is the opposite consideration.
questions.trap: Friction loss and water hammer both argue for a *lower* velocity, so they set the maximum, not the minimum.
questions.trick: Minimum velocity is always about keeping solids moving.

questions.q: The function of a forebay in a hydropower scheme is to:
o: Balance short-term fluctuations between the headrace supply and the turbine demand
Dissipate the energy of the tailrace flow
Remove the dissolved load from the water
Increase the gross head of the scheme
questions.s: It holds a small volume so that a sudden increase in turbine demand is met at once while the headrace catches up.
questions.trap: A surge tank also absorbs transients, but on a pressure tunnel rather than at the end of an open channel.
questions.trick: Forebay for an open headrace, surge tank for a pressure tunnel.

questions.q: In which turbine is all the available pressure energy converted into kinetic energy before the water strikes the runner?
questions.s: The nozzle converts the whole head into a free jet at atmospheric pressure; the runner then changes only the momentum of that jet.
questions.trap: Francis and Kaplan are reaction turbines in which pressure continues to drop *through* the runner.
questions.trick: Impulse converts first, reaction converts throughout.
questions.mn: Pelton: all kinetic at the nozzle.

questions.q: A spread foundation distributes the structural load by:
o: Increasing the bearing area so the pressure on the soil is reduced
Transferring the load to a deeper stratum
Developing skin friction along its sides
questions.s: Pressure is load divided by area, so a wider base brings the bearing pressure within the safe value of the soil immediately beneath it.
questions.trap: Transferring load to a deeper stratum is what a *pile* does, and both are foundations for weak ground.
questions.trick: Spread means spread out sideways, not down.
questions.mn: Spread the load, drop the pressure.

questions.q: Corporate income tax in Nepal is levied on a company's:
questions.s: Tax is charged on income after allowable expenses and depreciation have been deducted, not on the money that passes through the business.
questions.trap: Value added tax is charged on turnover, which makes gross revenue the natural but wrong basis here.
questions.trick: Income tax taxes income, and income is what is left after costs.

questions.q: The most likely mode of failure of a weir founded on a pervious foundation is:
o: Piping caused by undermining of the subsoil
questions.s: Seepage emerging at the downstream end carries soil particles away; as the channel works backwards the floor loses support and the structure settles.
questions.trap: Overturning and sliding govern gravity dams on rock, where seepage through the foundation is not the issue.
questions.trick: Pervious foundation means seepage, and seepage means piping.

questions.q: In Taylor's stability number Sn = Cm/(γH), the term Cm is:
questions.s: Cm is the cohesion actually required to keep the slope standing — the available cohesion divided by the factor of safety.
questions.trap: Cohesion at failure is the *available* value c; the mobilised value is what the slope is calling on.
questions.trick: Mobilised means in use, not in reserve.

questions.q: The shear strength of a saturated clay under undrained conditions is governed by:
o: The angle of internal friction alone
questions.s: Under rapid loading no drainage occurs, so the pore pressure takes the whole stress increase and the strength envelope is horizontal: s = cu.
questions.trap: The long-term (drained) strength of the same clay does have a friction angle, which makes "both" look safe.
questions.trick: No drainage, no change in effective stress, no friction mobilised.

questions.q: The allowable bearing capacity of a soil is also known as the:
questions.s: It is the lesser of the safe bearing capacity (strength, with a factor of safety) and the pressure that keeps settlement within tolerable limits.
questions.trap: Safe bearing capacity accounts only for shear failure; allowable adds the settlement check, which often governs.
questions.trick: Allowable must satisfy both strength and settlement.

questions.q: The metacentric height of a floating body is given by:
questions.s: BM = I/V is the distance from the centre of buoyancy to the metacentre; subtracting BG gives the metacentric height measured from the centre of gravity.
questions.trap: Adding BG instead of subtracting it would make every body more stable the higher its centre of gravity.
questions.trick: Raising G must reduce GM, so BG has to be subtracted.
questions.mn: GM = BM − BG, with BM = I/V. Positive means stable.

questions.q: The condition Q²T/(gA³) = 1 in an open channel describes:
questions.s: That expression is the Froude number squared written in terms of discharge; equal to one means critical flow and minimum specific energy.
questions.trap: Uniform flow is defined by the slope relation, not by this one, and is the commoner term.
questions.trick: Fr = 1 is critical, by definition.

questions.q: On a Mohr's circle, the minimum normal stress is:
o: The average of σ₁ and σ₃
questions.s: The circle runs between σ₃ and σ₁ on the normal-stress axis, so its leftmost point is the minimum normal stress — the minor principal stress.
questions.trap: The average of the two principal stresses is the *centre* of the circle, not its minimum.
questions.trick: Principal stresses are the extremes of normal stress, by definition.

questions.q: Whistle-blowing by an engineer is done to:
o: Disclose a danger to the public that the employer will not address
questions.s: It is justified when there is serious, probable harm, when internal channels have failed, and when the engineer has good evidence.
questions.trap: Protecting the employer is the usual professional duty; whistle-blowing is the case where a higher duty overrides it.
questions.trick: The test is harm to the public, not advantage to anyone.

questions.q: The influence line diagram for the reaction at a support of a simply supported beam is:
o: A triangle with unit ordinate at that support
questions.s: When the unit load stands over the support, that support carries all of it; when it stands at the far end, it carries none — so the diagram falls linearly from 1 to 0.
questions.trap: Bending moment influence lines are also triangular, but with the peak under the section rather than at a support.
questions.trick: Place the unit load at each end and join the two values.
questions.mn: Reaction ILD: 1 at its own support, 0 at the other.

questions.q: The float of an activity is:
o: The time it can be delayed without delaying the project
The time between its early and late start of the project
The time saved by crashing it
questions.s: Total float is the latest finish minus the earliest finish; using it does not move the project completion date.
questions.trap: Free float is the delay that does not disturb the *following activity* — a stricter and smaller quantity.
questions.trick: Float is spare time, measured against the project end.

questions.q: The total float of an activity on the critical path is:
questions.s: The critical path has no spare time anywhere along it; that is what makes it critical and what makes it the longest path.
questions.trap: Free float is also zero on the critical path, so both statements are true — but total float is what is asked.
questions.trick: Any float at all and the activity cannot be critical.

questions.q: The California bearing ratio test is carried out to assess:
o: The strength of a subgrade for pavement thickness design
The bitumen content of a mix
questions.s: CBR compares the load to penetrate a soil sample with that for standard crushed stone and is the basis of empirical pavement thickness design.
questions.trap: The plate load test also measures subgrade support, but gives the modulus of subgrade reaction used for *rigid* pavements.
questions.trick: CBR for flexible pavements, k-value for rigid.

questions.q: The maximum compressive strain in concrete at the limit state of collapse in bending is taken as:
questions.s: IS 456 fixes the extreme fibre compressive strain at 0.0035 in flexure; the strain at the onset of the constant-stress part of the curve is 0.002.
questions.trap: 0.002 is the strain at which the design stress block reaches its maximum, so it appears in the same diagram.
questions.trick: 0.002 is where the curve flattens, 0.0035 is where it ends.

questions.q: The maximum permissible aggregate impact value for a bituminous wearing course is:
questions.s: A wearing course takes the direct wheel impact, so the limit is the strictest at 30%; base courses are allowed 45% or more.
questions.trap: 45% is the limit for the lower layers and is the figure most often quoted.
questions.trick: The nearer the surface, the stronger the aggregate must be.

questions.q: The critical shear stress required to move a particle on a canal bed is expressed through the dimensionless Shields parameter, whose value for coarse sediment is about:
questions.s: Shields' curve flattens to roughly 0.056 for fully rough turbulent flow, and that constant is used in tractive force design.
questions.trap: The decimal point is the entire question — all four options carry the same digits.
questions.trick: The Shields parameter is a small fraction, a little above one twentieth.

questions.q: Failure of a flexible pavement that originates in the subgrade appears at the surface as:
questions.s: Excessive vertical strain at the top of the subgrade accumulates with repeated loading and shows as a depression in the wheel track.
questions.trap: Fatigue cracking is the other subgrade-related criterion, but it is caused by tensile strain at the bottom of the bituminous layer.
questions.trick: Subgrade criterion = vertical strain = rutting.

questions.q: Slenderness ratio is considered in the design of a steel compression member because it governs:
o: The buckling strength of the member
The tensile capacity of the member
The bearing strength of the bolts
questions.s: A slender column fails by buckling long before the material yields, so the permissible stress falls as the slenderness ratio rises.
questions.trap: Slenderness has no effect on tensile capacity, because a tension member cannot buckle.
questions.trick: Slenderness only matters when the force pushes.

questions.q: Portland pozzolana cement is particularly resistant to attack by:
questions.s: The pozzolana consumes free lime and reduces C3A, which is what sulphates attack; PPC is therefore preferred for marine and sewage works.
questions.trap: PPC also helps with the alkali-aggregate reaction, which makes that option partly right — its defining advantage is sulphate resistance.
questions.trick: Less free lime and less C3A means less for sulphate to attack.

questions.q: The minimum compressive strength of a first-class brick is:
questions.s: A first-class brick must reach at least 10.5 N/mm²; a second-class brick 7.5 N/mm², and the common building brick 3.5 N/mm².
questions.trap: 3.5 N/mm² is the minimum for *any* burnt clay brick and is widely quoted, which makes it the usual wrong answer.
questions.trick: The class numbers run down as the strength does: 10.5, 7.5, 3.5.

questions.q: An aquifer that is bounded above and below by impervious layers and is under pressure is called:
questions.s: Water in a confined aquifer stands above the top of the formation when a well is sunk, because it is under pressure greater than atmospheric.
questions.trap: A leaky (semi-confined) aquifer has a partly permeable boundary, so it is confined only in part.
questions.trick: Confined above and below, and therefore pressurised.

questions.q: In seismic design, the importance factor for a hospital or other lifeline structure is:
o: Greater than that for an ordinary building
Equal to that for an ordinary building
Less than that for an ordinary building
questions.s: Lifeline buildings must remain serviceable after an earthquake, so the design force is raised by an importance factor of 1.5 against 1.0 for ordinary buildings.
questions.trap: A larger factor feels like a penalty on the designer; it is a deliberate increase in required performance.
questions.trick: The more important the building, the larger the design force.

questions.q: A concentrated load applied to the flange of a steel beam is assumed to disperse into the web at:
questions.s: The dispersion of a concentrated load through the flange into the web is taken at 1:1, which is 45° — the basis of the web crippling check.
questions.trap: Load dispersion through a concrete slab is often taken at 30° or 1:2, which is the number carried across from the other material.
questions.trick: Steel disperses at 45°; concrete at 1:2.

questions.q: In an isometric drawing, the height of an object is measured along the:
questions.s: The three isometric axes are one vertical and two at 30° to the horizontal; height is always set out on the vertical one.
questions.trap: The two 30° axes carry length and width, and they are the ones that make the drawing look isometric.
questions.trick: Height is vertical in every projection, isometric included.
questions.mn: Up is up, even in isometric.

questions.q: In a surveying telescope, the real inverted image is formed:
o: At the plane of the diaphragm (cross hairs)
questions.s: The objective forms a real image in the plane of the cross hairs, and the eyepiece then magnifies image and hairs together.
questions.trap: Forming the image at the eyepiece would mean the cross hairs could never be in focus with it.
questions.trick: The image must coincide with the hairs, or there would be parallax.
questions.mn: Image on the hairs — no parallax.

questions.q: Project risk management consists of:
o: Identifying, analysing, responding to and monitoring risk
Transferring all risk to the contractor
questions.s: It is a continuous cycle: identify what could go wrong, assess likelihood and impact, plan a response, then monitor as the project proceeds.
questions.trap: Insurance and transfer are *responses* to risk, so each is one part of the third step rather than the whole process.
questions.trick: Risk management is a process, not a product you can buy.

questions.q: In a waterlogged area, capillary rise:
o: Brings salts to the surface and leaves them there as the water evaporates
Increases the permeability of the soil
questions.s: Water drawn up by capillarity evaporates at the surface and leaves its dissolved salts behind, so the land becomes saline as well as waterlogged.
questions.trap: Capillary rise does bring moisture to the root zone, which sounds beneficial until the salt is accounted for.
questions.trick: The water leaves; the salt does not.

questions.q: Capillary rise in a fine tube is caused by:
o: Surface tension together with adhesion to the tube wall
questions.s: h = 4σcosθ/(ρgd) — the rise is proportional to surface tension and inversely proportional to the tube diameter.
questions.trap: Viscosity governs how fast the liquid rises, not how far — a common conflation.
questions.trick: Narrower tube, higher rise; that points straight at surface tension.
questions.mn: Capillarity is surface tension at work.

questions.q: To be registered as a professional engineer with the NEC, a person must hold:
o: A recognised engineering degree and the prescribed professional experience
Only a certificate of practice from an employer
questions.s: Registration requires a degree from an institution recognised by the Council together with the experience its regulations prescribe for the category.
questions.trap: A diploma qualifies a person as an associate or sub-engineer, not a professional engineer.
questions.trick: The category of registration follows the level of qualification.

questions.q: The Sustainable Development Goals comprise:
questions.s: The 2030 Agenda sets 17 goals and 169 targets; the indicators that measure them number about 230.
questions.trap: 230 is the number of *indicators*, offered beside the targets to see whether the two are told apart.
questions.trick: Goals 17, targets 169, indicators about 230.

questions.q: The stopping sight distance for a design speed of 80 km/h on a level road is about:
questions.s: SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f) with t = 2.5 s and f = 0.35 gives roughly 120 m at 80 km/h.
questions.trap: Doubling the speed does not double the distance — the braking term is proportional to V², which is why estimates come out low.
questions.trick: The braking term grows with the square of the speed.

questions.q: The distance travelled between the moment a driver sees an object and the moment the brakes are applied is the:
questions.s: Lag (reaction) distance is the speed multiplied by the perception-reaction time, usually 2.5 s. Adding the braking distance gives the stopping sight distance.
questions.trap: Braking distance is the part after the brakes bite, and together the two make up the SSD.
questions.trick: Lag first, brake second, SSD is the sum.

questions.q: Time headway is measured in:
questions.s: Time headway is the interval between successive vehicles passing a point; space headway, measured in metres, is the distance between them.
questions.trap: Space headway is the related quantity measured in metres, and the word "headway" alone does not say which is meant.
questions.trick: Time headway is a time, so it is in seconds.
questions.mn: Time headway, seconds; space headway, metres.

questions.q: The strain energy stored in a member of length L subjected to a constant bending moment M is:
questions.s: U = ∫M²dx/2EI; with M constant the integral is simply M²L/2EI.
questions.trap: ML²/2EI has the right look but the wrong powers — it is dimensionally not an energy.
questions.trick: Strain energy always carries the load squared.

questions.q: For a series of moving wheel loads on a simply supported girder, the absolute maximum bending moment occurs:
questions.s: It occurs under the load that is placed so that the centre line of the span bisects the distance between that load and the resultant of the whole system.
questions.trap: Mid-span is where the maximum sits for a single central load, so it is the answer carried over by habit.
questions.trick: The maximum always occurs *under a load*, not in the gap between them.
questions.mn: Bisect between the load and the resultant.

questions.q: A level crossing is the intersection of a road with:
o: A railway at the same level
Another road at a different level
questions.s: It is a road-rail intersection at grade, controlled by gates or signals because the two cannot pass at the same time.
questions.trap: A road-over-road intersection at the same level is simply an at-grade junction, not a level crossing.
questions.trick: "Level" refers to the grade; the crossing is with a railway.

questions.q: An aqueduct is a cross-drainage work in which:
o: The canal is carried over the drainage
The drainage is carried over the canal
The two flows are allowed to mix
The canal passes under the drainage in a barrel
questions.s: Canal over drain is an aqueduct; drain over canal is a super-passage; mixing them is a level crossing.
questions.trap: A super-passage is the mirror image and the two names give no clue which way round they go.
questions.trick: Think of a Roman aqueduct — the water channel is carried up on arches.

questions.q: The kinematic indeterminacy of a plane truss joint is:
questions.s: Truss members carry axial force only, so joint rotation is not a degree of freedom; each free joint has two translations in a plane.
questions.trap: A plane *frame* joint has three degrees of freedom, and that figure is carried across to the truss.
questions.trick: No moment at a pin, so no rotational freedom to count.

questions.q: In a nailed timber joint, the minimum spacing of nails along the grain in a tension member is about:
questions.s: Tension members need wider nail spacing than compression members — about 10d along the grain against roughly 5d in compression — because splitting is the governing failure.
questions.trap: The compression spacing is smaller, so quoting it here under-spaces the joint and invites a split.
questions.trick: Tension splits timber, so the fasteners must be kept further apart.

questions.q: A professional engineer should NOT:
o: Accept work outside their field of competence
Keep up to date with technical developments
Report a danger to public safety
Decline work for which they are not qualified
questions.s: Every code of conduct limits an engineer to work within their competence; accepting work beyond it endangers the public and the profession.
questions.trap: The other three are positive duties, written to look like candidate prohibitions.
questions.trick: Only one of the four would harm anyone.

questions.q: Which valve is provided at a summit in a pipeline to release accumulated air?
questions.s: Air collects at high points and throttles the flow; an air valve lets it escape. A scour valve at the low points removes sediment.
questions.trap: The scour valve is the exact counterpart at the bottom of the profile, and the pair are routinely swapped.
questions.trick: Air rises, sediment sinks — valve each at its own end.
questions.mn: Air at the top, scour at the bottom.

questions.q: Which pipe material is preferred for high-pressure water mains?
questions.s: Steel has high tensile strength and ductility, so it carries high internal pressure in thinner walls than brittle materials can.
questions.trap: Cast iron is the traditional water main material, but it is brittle and limited to moderate pressures.
questions.trick: High pressure means hoop tension, and tension means steel.

questions.q: Stoneware sewer pipes are jointed using:
o: A cement mortar collar joint with a tarred gasket
questions.s: The spigot is centred in the socket on a jute or tarred gasket and the remaining space filled with cement mortar.
questions.trap: Flanged and welded joints belong to metal pipes, which cannot be used for the corrosive contents of a sewer.
questions.trick: A brittle ceramic pipe can only take a packed joint.

questions.q: A separate sewerage system is preferred where:
o: Rainfall is heavy and sewage must be treated
The town has a flat gradient
questions.s: Keeping storm water out keeps the treatment works small; in a combined system every storm would swamp it.
questions.trap: A combined system is cheaper to build, which makes it the right answer to the *cost* question but not to this one.
questions.trick: Treatment capacity is what decides it: never pay to treat rainwater.

questions.q: A guide bund is provided to:
o: Confine and guide the river flow through a bridge or weir opening
Raise the water level for diversion
Trap sediment upstream of the intake
questions.s: Guide bunds hold the river to a defined width across the structure and prevent it outflanking the works.
questions.trap: A spur also protects a bank, but it projects into the flow instead of guiding it along a prepared line.
questions.trick: Guide bunds guide; spurs deflect.
questions.mn: Guide the river through the gap.

questions.q: The main effect of installing a traffic signal at an intersection is to:
o: Separate conflicting movements in time and reduce right-angle collisions
Increase the capacity of every approach
Remove the need for road markings
questions.s: Signals assign right of way by time rather than by driver judgement. Total delay often rises even as serious collisions fall.
questions.trap: "Increases capacity" is the expectation, but a signal gives each approach only part of the time and can reduce total capacity.
questions.trick: Signals trade delay for safety.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT considered in the geometric design of a highway?
o: The thickness of the pavement layers
questions.s: Geometric design settles the shape of the road — alignment, cross-section, sight distance. Layer thickness belongs to pavement design.
questions.trap: Both are part of designing a road, which makes the boundary between them the whole question.
questions.trick: Geometry is what you would see on a drawing of the road surface.
questions.mn: Shape is geometric, thickness is structural.

questions.q: In a reinforced concrete member, steel and concrete act together mainly because:
o: Their coefficients of thermal expansion are nearly equal and bond develops between them
They have the same modulus of elasticity
questions.s: Nearly equal thermal expansion (about 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C) means temperature changes do not break the bond, and the bond makes them strain together.
questions.trap: Their moduli differ by a factor of about eight, which is precisely why the modular ratio exists.
questions.trick: If the expansions differed, the first hot day would destroy the bond.

questions.q: The property by which a material regains its original shape after the load is removed is:
questions.s: Elasticity is complete recovery on unloading; plasticity is the retention of deformation after the load is taken off.
questions.trap: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into a wire, which also involves deformation but permanent deformation.
questions.trick: Recovery means elastic; retention means plastic.

questions.q: The property by which strain continues to disappear slowly after the load has been removed is called:
questions.s: The elastic after-effect is the time lag in recovering the strain; creep is the opposite, a slow increase in strain while the load is sustained.
questions.trap: Creep happens under constant load, after-effect happens after unloading — the two are mirror images.
questions.trick: Ask whether the load is still on.
questions.mn: Load on: creep. Load off: after-effect.

questions.q: On the stress-strain curve of mild steel, the point immediately after the ultimate stress is:
o: The breaking (rupture) point, reached after necking
questions.s: Past the ultimate stress the specimen necks, the true area falls rapidly, and the nominal stress declines until fracture.
questions.trap: Yield, elastic limit and proportional limit all come *before* the ultimate stress, not after it.
questions.trick: Only one point on the curve lies beyond the peak.

questions.q: The shrinkage limit of a soil is:
o: The water content below which no further volume reduction occurs on drying
The water content at which the soil flows
The water content at which the soil crumbles when rolled
The maximum water content a soil can hold
questions.s: At and below the shrinkage limit the voids stay the same size while water continues to leave, so the volume is constant.
questions.trap: Rolling into a thread defines the plastic limit, which is the next Atterberg limit above it.
questions.trick: It is the only limit defined by a change in volume rather than in behaviour.

questions.q: For a two-hinged semicircular arch carrying a point load, the locus of the reaction at a support is:
questions.s: The horizontal and vertical components vary in fixed proportion as the load moves, so the resultant reaction traces a straight line.
questions.trap: The arch is semicircular, which tempts the eye towards a circular locus.
questions.trick: A locus of a resultant of two linearly related components is always straight.

questions.q: For a semicircular lamina, the centre of gravity lies:
o: Inside the lamina, on the axis of symmetry
At the centre of the full circle
questions.s: It lies on the axis of symmetry at 4R/3π from the diameter, which is inside the material.
questions.trap: The centroid of a *ring* or an angle section can indeed fall outside the material, which is where this idea comes from.
questions.trick: For any solid convex shape, the centroid must lie within it.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of a quadrant of a circle of radius R lies from each straight edge at:
questions.s: By symmetry it is 4R/3π from both radii — the same distance as the semicircular lamina from its diameter.
questions.trap: 2R/3π is half the right value and appears in the same family of results.
questions.trick: The quadrant shares the semicircle's centroidal distance, taken about both edges.

questions.q: In the sum-of-years-digits method of depreciation over a 4-year life, the sum of the digits is:
questions.s: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, so the first year's depreciation is 4/10 of the depreciable value and the last year's is 1/10.
questions.trap: 24 is 4 factorial and 16 is 4 squared — both plausible-looking arithmetic on the number 4.
questions.mn: Add the years, do not multiply them.

questions.q: An open (shallow) foundation is used where:
o: Firm soil of adequate capacity is available at a shallow depth
The soil is weak for a great depth
The structure is subject to large uplift
The water table is very high
questions.s: It is excavated in open cut and built in place, which is only economical while the bearing stratum is near the surface.
questions.trap: Weak soil to great depth is exactly the case that forces a *deep* foundation instead.
questions.trick: Open means dug out in the open, which limits how deep it can go.
questions.mn: Good soil near the top, open footing.

questions.q: Effective communication in a construction project is important mainly because it:
o: Prevents misunderstanding between the parties and reduces disputes
Replaces the need for written contracts
questions.s: Most construction disputes begin as a misunderstanding of scope, instruction or expectation, which clear and recorded communication prevents.
questions.trap: Communication supports a contract; it never replaces one.
questions.trick: The benefit is fewer disputes, not cheaper materials.

questions.q: Watershed deterioration is caused mainly by:
questions.s: Removing vegetation exposes the soil, so runoff and erosion rise and the catchment loses its ability to regulate flow.
questions.trap: The other three options are all *remedies* for the same problem, offered as if they were causes.
questions.trick: Pick the one that removes vegetation rather than adds it.
questions.mn: Lose the trees, lose the watershed.

questions.q: A canal is designed for a velocity that is:
o: Equal to the critical velocity of the flow
questions.s: Too low and sediment settles; too high and the bed and banks erode. Kennedy's and Lacey's theories both aim at the regime between the two.
questions.trap: "Critical velocity" in Kennedy's sense is the non-silting velocity, which is only half the requirement.
questions.trick: The design velocity is a band, not a maximum or a minimum.

questions.q: A piston sampler is used to obtain:
questions.s: The piston keeps the tube sealed on the way down and holds the sample by suction on the way up, which is what soft clay needs.
questions.trap: A split-spoon sampler is the familiar one from the SPT, and it returns a *disturbed* sample.
questions.trick: Undisturbed sampling of soft soil needs a thin wall and a piston.

questions.q: The coefficient of earth pressure at rest K₀ for a normally consolidated soil is given by:
questions.s: Jaky's expression K₀ = 1 − sinφ applies when there has been no lateral strain at all.
questions.trap: (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ) is the *active* coefficient, which applies only after the wall has yielded away from the soil.
questions.trick: At rest means nothing has moved, so Ka does not apply.

questions.q: When total stress on a saturated clay is increased rapidly, the immediate effect is:
o: The pore water pressure rises by the whole increment
The effective stress rises by the whole increment
questions.s: Water cannot escape at once, so it carries the whole of the increase; effective stress rises only as the excess pore pressure dissipates.
questions.trap: In sand the pore pressure dissipates almost instantly, so the intuition from granular soils gives the wrong answer here.
questions.trick: Water is incompressible and cannot leave quickly, so it takes the load first.
questions.mn: Load first to the water, then to the grains.

questions.q: Kennedy's critical velocity ratio depends on:
o: The type and grade of the silt carried
The bed slope of the canal
The side slope of the canal
questions.s: The critical velocity ratio m adjusts Kennedy's formula for silt coarser or finer than the Upper Bari Doab material it was derived from.
questions.trap: Bed slope governs the velocity itself, so it is easily mistaken for what the ratio corrects.
questions.trick: The ratio corrects for the sediment, not for the geometry.

questions.q: In a stair, the handrail is connected to the:
questions.s: The balusters stand on the string or the treads and carry the handrail, which terminates against the newel post at each change of direction.
questions.trap: Treads and risers are the walking surfaces and carry no part of the rail.
questions.trick: Follow the load path: rail to baluster to string or newel.
questions.mn: Newel and balusters hold the rail.

questions.q: Night soil is another name for:
o: Human excreta collected without water carriage
questions.s: It is the excreta collected in a conservancy system, so called because it was removed at night.
questions.trap: Sullage is the waste water from kitchens and baths and contains no excreta, which is precisely the distinction.
questions.trick: Sullage has no faecal matter; sewage and night soil do.
questions.mn: Night soil is excreta; sullage is wash water.

questions.q: Alkalinity in natural water is chiefly due to:
questions.s: These three ions give water its capacity to neutralise acid, and bicarbonate dominates at normal pH.
questions.trap: Chlorides and sulphates contribute to hardness and to taste, but neither buffers acid.
questions.trick: Alkalinity is an acid-neutralising capacity, so it must come from basic ions.

questions.q: The lime-soda process is used for:
questions.s: Lime removes carbonate hardness and soda ash removes non-carbonate hardness, both by precipitating calcium and magnesium.
questions.trap: Alum removes turbidity and chlorine disinfects — each stage of a treatment works has its own chemical.
questions.trick: Lime and soda both target hardness ions.

questions.q: In the conventional activated sludge process, the returned sludge is about:
questions.s: Returning a quarter to a half of the flow maintains the mixed liquor suspended solids at the design concentration.
questions.trap: Extended aeration and other modifications use far higher return ratios, so larger figures are not absurd.
questions.trick: The return keeps the biomass up without doubling the tank throughput.
questions.mn: Return a quarter to a half.

questions.q: The piezometric head at a point is equal to:
o: The pressure head plus the datum head
The velocity head plus the datum head
questions.s: It is the level to which water rises in a piezometer, which measures pressure and elevation but not velocity.
questions.trap: Total head adds the velocity head, and in a slow-moving flow the two are nearly equal — but not identical.
questions.trick: A piezometer is open and still, so it cannot register velocity head.

questions.q: The irrigation interval (frequency) is equal to:
o: The net depth of water available in the root zone divided by the peak daily consumptive use
The base period divided by the delta
The delta multiplied by the duty
The duty divided by the base period
questions.s: The soil holds a certain depth of readily available water; dividing by the rate at which the crop uses it gives the days between waterings.
questions.trap: Delta, duty and base period are related to one another by their own formula, which is a different relation entirely.
questions.trick: Interval is a storage divided by a rate, so it comes out in days.

questions.q: The crest of the under-sluices is kept:
o: Lower than the crest of the head regulator
Higher than the crest of the head regulator
At the same level as the head regulator
questions.s: Keeping the under-sluice crest low forms a still pocket in front of the head regulator, so the coarse sediment settles there and is scoured away through the sluices.
questions.trap: Setting both crests level would let the bed load travel straight into the canal.
questions.trick: Sediment collects at the lowest point, so put the scouring outlet there.

questions.q: A power plant with a high operating cost but great flexibility is best used for:
questions.s: Peaking plant runs for only a few hours a day, so a high running cost matters little; what matters is how quickly it can start and stop.
questions.trap: Base load plant is the opposite case: low running cost, poor flexibility, run continuously.
questions.trick: Few hours of operation make capital and flexibility matter more than fuel cost.

questions.q: The main factor in selecting a plant for peak load service is its:
o: Ability to start and change output quickly
questions.s: A peaking plant must come on line within minutes and follow a rapidly changing demand.
questions.trap: Lowest cost per unit is exactly the criterion for *base* load plant, which runs all the time.
questions.trick: Peaking is about speed of response, not economy.
questions.mn: Peaking plant is chosen for speed, base load for cheapness.

questions.q: The area under a daily load curve represents:
o: The total energy generated in the day
questions.s: Power multiplied by time is energy, so the area beneath the curve is the number of units supplied over the day.
questions.trap: The maximum demand is the *peak* of the curve, a single ordinate rather than an area.
questions.trick: Area under a power-time plot is always energy.

questions.q: A double mass curve is used to:
o: Check the consistency of a rainfall record
Route a flood through a reservoir
questions.s: Plotting the cumulative rainfall of one station against the cumulative mean of surrounding stations gives a straight line; a change in slope shows the record has been disturbed.
questions.trap: A mass curve on its own is used for reservoir storage calculations, which is a different plot with a similar name.
questions.trick: "Double" means two cumulative totals plotted against each other.

questions.q: A gravity dam is preferred on a foundation of:
questions.s: The whole weight of the dam is carried on a narrow base, so the foundation must take high bearing pressure and resist sliding — which only sound rock does.
questions.trap: An earthen dam is the one that can be founded on soil, and that flexibility is easy to transfer to the wrong dam type.
questions.trick: Concrete dam, rock foundation; earth dam, soil foundation.

questions.q: A newly laid rigid (cement concrete) pavement is normally opened to traffic after:
questions.s: Concrete reaches its characteristic strength at 28 days, and only then can the slab carry its design wheel load.
questions.trap: 7 days is the usual curing period, after which the surface is firm — but the concrete has only about two-thirds of its strength.
questions.trick: Curing period and opening time are not the same thing.

questions.q: The rate of change of bending moment with respect to distance along a beam is equal to:
questions.s: dM/dx = V, and differentiating once more gives dV/dx = −w.
questions.trap: The load intensity is the derivative of the *shear force*, one step further along the same chain.
questions.trick: Load → shear → moment, each by one integration.

questions.q: The flow in a penstock or any large pressure pipe is almost always:
questions.s: Reynolds numbers in a penstock run into the millions, far above the transition value of about 2000.
questions.trap: Laminar flow is the case analysed first in every textbook, so it is the more familiar word.
questions.trick: Large diameter and high velocity both drive Re up.

questions.q: In a mass haul diagram, a falling (negative) ordinate indicates:
questions.s: The curve accumulates cut as positive and fill as negative, so a falling section means earth is being placed rather than removed.
questions.trap: Cut and fill are offered together and the sign convention is the entire question.
questions.trick: Rising means earth is being won; falling means it is being used.
questions.mn: Up is cut, down is fill.

questions.q: A pressure relief valve in a pipeline is provided to:
o: Protect the pipe from excessive internal pressure
questions.s: It opens automatically when the pressure exceeds a set value and discharges enough water to bring it back down.
questions.trap: Admitting air during emptying is the duty of an air valve, which also sits at the top of the main.
questions.trick: A relief valve relieves pressure.

questions.q: When a floating block of ice melts in a container of water, the water level:
questions.s: Floating ice displaces its own weight of water, and on melting it produces exactly that weight of water, so the volume displaced is unchanged.
questions.trap: Ice is less dense, so it looks as though melting must reduce the volume and lower the level.
questions.trick: Compare weights, not volumes: the displaced weight equals the ice weight either way.
questions.mn: Floating ice melts to its own displacement.

questions.q: Minimum shear reinforcement in a beam is provided in the form of:
o: Vertical stirrups at a prescribed maximum spacing
Extra longitudinal bars at the bottom
Additional cover to the main steel
questions.s: IS 456 requires Asv/(b·sv) ≥ 0.4/0.87fy, so that a beam always has some stirrups even where the calculated shear is small.
questions.trap: Bent-up bars can carry shear but are never allowed to provide more than half of it, so they cannot supply the minimum alone.
questions.trick: The minimum is about guaranteeing stirrups everywhere.

questions.q: The exit head loss at a submerged outlet from a pipe into a large reservoir is:
o: V²/2g — the whole velocity head is lost
questions.s: The jet dissipates in the still water of the reservoir, so all the kinetic energy it carried is lost.
questions.trap: 0.5V²/2g is the *entrance* loss for a sharp-edged pipe, the mirror case at the other end.
questions.trick: Entry costs half a velocity head, exit costs a whole one.

questions.q: The hardening of cement is due to:
questions.s: Water reacts chemically with the silicates and aluminates to form the hydrated gel that binds the mix. Drying out stops the reaction.
questions.trap: Concrete does dry as it hardens, which makes evaporation look like the cause rather than an unwanted side effect.
questions.trick: If evaporation hardened concrete, curing would not require keeping it wet.

questions.q: The value of a property estimated without dismantling or physically testing it is called:
questions.s: A valuer forms an opinion from inspection, measurement and comparison with similar properties; nothing is taken apart.
questions.trap: Scrap value is what the materials fetch after demolition — the opposite situation.
questions.trick: Scrap and salvage both assume the building has come down.

questions.q: The degree of saturation of a fully saturated soil is:
questions.s: All the voids are filled with water, so the volume of water equals the volume of voids and S = 1.
questions.trap: A saturation above 100% is impossible, since water cannot exceed the space available.
questions.trick: S is a ratio of water volume to void volume, so it can never exceed one.

questions.q: The minimum percentage of tension reinforcement in an RCC beam as per IS 456 is:
questions.s: As/(bd) shall not be less than 0.85/fy, which gives about 0.205% for Fe415 steel.
questions.trap: 0.12% is the minimum for a *slab* with high-strength deformed bars, a figure from the same code and the same chapter.
questions.trick: Beams use a formula in fy; slabs use a flat percentage.

questions.q: In highway planning, the saturation system considers:
o: The utility of each road to the area it serves, scored by population and produce
questions.s: Each proposed road is scored by the population served and the agricultural and industrial produce carried, and the roads are built in order of merit.
questions.trap: Cost and existing traffic are inputs to many planning methods, but the saturation system is built on utility units.
questions.trick: It saturates the area with the roads that serve the most people and goods.
questions.mn: Utility per road decides the order.

questions.q: A person may practise engineering in Nepal only after:
o: Obtaining registration and a certificate from the Nepal Engineering Council
questions.s: The NEC Act makes registration a precondition of practice; a degree alone is not sufficient.
questions.trap: A degree is a *requirement for* registration, which makes it look sufficient on its own.
questions.trick: Qualification and license are two separate steps.

questions.q: As per NBC, the standard size of a brick in Nepal is:
questions.s: The Nepal Building Code gives 240 × 115 × 57 mm, which with a 10 mm joint makes a modular 250 × 125 × 67 mm.
questions.trap: 230 × 110 × 55 mm is the Indian standard brick, and the two differ by only a few millimetres.
questions.trick: Add the 10 mm mortar joint and the Nepali brick comes to a round 250 mm.

questions.q: The relationship between the flexural strength and the characteristic compressive strength of concrete as per IS 456 is:
questions.s: The modulus of rupture is taken as 0.7√fck in newtons per square millimetre, which is used in the deflection and cracking checks.
questions.trap: 5000√fck is the modulus of elasticity — the same square root in the same code, but a stiffness rather than a strength.
questions.trick: 0.7 for rupture, 5000 for elasticity.

questions.q: The theoretical power in kilowatts available from a discharge Q in m³/s under a net head H in metres is:
questions.s: P = ρgQH = 1000 × 9.81 × Q × H watts, which is 9.81QH kilowatts before efficiency is applied.
questions.trap: 1000QH forgets g; the other two options move the decimal point by a factor of ten in each direction.
questions.trick: Divide the watt expression by 1000 and ρ cancels against it, leaving g.
questions.mn: Power in kilowatts is 9.81 QH, before efficiency.

questions.q: According to Khosla’s theory, the exit gradient in the absence of a downstream cut-off is:
questions.s: With no vertical cut-off the seepage path ends abruptly at the floor, and the mathematics returns an infinite exit gradient — which is why a downstream cut-off is always provided.
questions.trap: Zero is the intuitive answer for “nothing there”, but removing the cut-off makes the condition worse, not safer.
questions.trick: The cut-off is what makes the exit gradient finite.
